questions.q: What is SSMS's job creation wizard actually doing under the hood?
options: Calling a fixed sequence of msdb system stored procedures — sp_add_job, sp_add_jobstep, sp_add_schedule, sp_attach_schedule, sp_add_jobserver — that can also be scripted directly
Directly editing binary configuration files with no stored procedures involved
Calling a single stored procedure that creates the entire job in one step
Making a call to an external Azure REST API regardless of platform
questions.explain: Knowing these procedures directly matters for scripting jobs for source control or repeating them across environments.

questions.q: What happens if a DBA creates a job and its steps and schedule but forgets to run sp_add_jobserver?
options: The job has no server target and never actually runs anywhere
The job runs automatically on every server in the Azure subscription
SQL Server Agent assigns a default server target automatically with no action needed
The job runs once immediately and then is deleted
questions.explain: sp_add_jobserver targets the job at a server — skipping it is a common, easy-to-forget mistake that leaves the job un-runnable.

questions.q: Why are on-success and on-fail actions set independently per job step rather than as a single setting for the whole job?
options: Because a multi-step job can define deliberate failure paths — e.g. jumping straight to an alerting step on failure instead of continuing into a rebuild against a database that just failed CHECKDB
Because SQL Server requires every step to have identical success and failure actions
Because only the final step in a job can have a failure action at all
Because on-success and on-fail actions only apply to PowerShell steps
questions.explain: Per-step control is what makes multi-step jobs more useful than one long script — each step can react differently to its own outcome.

questions.q: Besides TSQL, what other subsystems can a job step use, per this lesson?
options: PowerShell, CmdExec (OS-level commands or executables), and SSIS packages
Only TSQL is supported as a step subsystem
Only PowerShell is supported as an alternative to TSQL
Python and Java are the only alternatives to TSQL
questions.explain: The @subsystem parameter is what makes Agent more than a T-SQL runner — a real maintenance job commonly mixes TSQL with PowerShell or CmdExec steps.

questions.q: Why is sp_attach_schedule a separate step from sp_add_schedule?
options: Because a schedule is a standalone, reusable object — one schedule (e.g. 'every night at 2 AM') can be attached to multiple unrelated jobs instead of redefining the same recurrence repeatedly
Because sp_add_schedule only creates a placeholder with no actual recurrence data
Because schedules can only ever be attached to exactly the job that created them
Because sp_attach_schedule is deprecated and should not be used
questions.explain: Separating schedule creation from attachment lets one schedule definition be shared across many jobs.
